title: Mindfulness of death
hook: a room of monks, each saying how long they count on living: a day, a meal, a mouthful, a breath
tomorrow: why would anyone compare the body to a sack of beans?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the six recollections with the bright ones, and the faith and giving that made them bright. Today's subject is the one that's easiest to skip.

Calendars, countdowns to summer, a reminder set for next Thursday: plans assume time. In one sutta the Buddha asks a room of monks how they keep death in mind. One says: I think, may I live a night and a day, to practice. Another: one day. Another: as long as it takes to eat a meal. Another: four or five mouthfuls. Another: one mouthful. And the last: the time it takes to breathe in, and out. The Buddha's answer runs backwards.
screen: `PLANS ASSUME TIME.` → `A DAY? A MEAL?` → `ONE MOUTHFUL. ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The day and the meal, he says, are heedless: still too slow. The one mouthful and the one breath, he praises. The point isn't gloom. It's precision. Death is certain; its hour isn't. The word is maranasati: marana, death, and sati, mindfulness. The Visuddhimagga makes it a meditation subject and gives ways to bring it close: death comes to the famous and the strong as well; a life hangs on breath, warmth and food. The manual also warns that done carelessly, it stirs up grief or fear, so it asks for mindfulness, urgency and understanding together. And the Dhammapada names the payoff. In Max Müller's translation: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." That's the surprise. Knowing time is short doesn't shrink a life. It shrinks the arguments. A text about death turns out to be about how you'll talk to your brother tonight.
screen: `A DAY IS TOO SLOW.` · `ONE BREATH IS PRAISED.` · `CERTAIN, BUT NOT WHEN.` · `THEIR QUARRELS CEASE.` · then, large: `DEATH IS CERTAIN.`

segments.voice: Rest a hand on your chest and feel one breath all the way through: the cool air in, the chest rising under your palm, the slow way out. As it leaves, notice that this breath wasn't promised, and it came anyway. Stay with the breaths like that, one at a time, each one received as it arrives.
Maranasati: mindfulness of death. Not dread, but a clear, gentle remembering that the time isn't promised. Praised, in the sutta, one breath at a time.
Carry this: death is certain, and today's quarrels can stay small. Day twenty-five of the forty.

howItsDone: Theravada monks and lay meditators practice mindfulness of death as one of the forty meditation subjects, and teachers give it with care so that it brings urgency rather than fear.

fork.setup: your cousin and her sister haven't spoken in weeks over a borrowed jacket. both say they'll make up 'eventually.' what does mindfulness of death say?
options: wait it out; there's plenty of time once things cool off.
the time isn't promised, so the fight is small. reach out now.
think about death until the fight feels pointless and numb.
fork.reveal: death is certain and its hour isn't, and the Dhammapada says those who know it let their quarrels cease. 'eventually' is the slow answer the sutta calls heedless.

original.note: Pali: marana, death, with sati, mindfulness; written maranasati in English too.

trapdoor: what you thought: thinking about dying until you feel sad.
what it means: remembering that death is certain and its hour isn't, so this breath, this meal, this conversation counts.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.19 praises recollecting death over one mouthful or one breath; Visuddhimagga 8 asks for mindfulness, urgency and understanding so it doesn't turn into grief or fear.
guess: keeping in mind, gently, that life will end
a ritual honoring relatives who have died
a vow to never fear death or anything else
recall: their bright qualities, in you too
calling your own gifts to mind, gladly

chat.says: ông showed me which bonsai is mine 'when i'm gone.' said it like the weather. i froze.
options: He's not being grim. Knowing time isn't promised can make the time you have together count more.
Change the subject fast. Talking about death just makes everybody sad for nothing.
Tell him not to say that. If you don't talk about it, it feels further away.
chat.meaning: Mindfulness of death isn't dread. Remembering that time isn't promised makes the quarrels smaller and the time together count.

tie.story: The Buddha praised keeping death in mind one breath at a time, and the Dhammapada says quarrels cease.
tie.friend: Mai can hear ông's calm as a gift, and stay for the afternoon.
tie.you: who would you talk to differently if time felt less promised?
